text: over 90% of bladder cancers are transitional cell in type. About two-thirds of all cases occur in men, and the median age at diagnosis is 65 years. Known risk factors include smoking and exposure to ani- line dyes. In countries where it is endemic, schistosomiasis is an important cause of squamous cell bladder cancer. Most patients present with haematuria; there may also be urinary frequency or dysuria. Urothelial tumours fall into 3 major groups, non-invasive, invasive, and metastatic, which differ in prognosis and management.1 About 70% of cases are non-muscle-inva- sive (superficial), 25% are muscle-invasive, and 5% are metastatic.2 Of the non-muscle invasive tumours, about 70% are low- grade transitional cell carcinomas confined to the mucosa (Ta), and have a low risk of progression to muscle invasive disease and a 50% chance of recurrence. Most of the re- mainder are higher-grade transitional cell carcinomas that have invaded the submucosa (T1), and a small percentage are high-grade carcinoma in situ (CIS). These high-grade tumours have a high risk of progression to muscle invasive disease, and a 50 to 90% chance of recurrence. The stand- ard initial treatment for primary or recurrent superficial disease is surgery, in the form of transurethral resection. In an attempt to prolong remission and reduce the recurrence rate antineoplastics have been instilled into the bladder af- ter complete resection (prophylactic or adjuvant intravesi- cal therapy).2 Effective agents include doxorubicin, epiru- bicin, mitomycin, and thiotepa. These increase the disease- free interval, but do not reduce the risk of progression to invasive disease, nor prolong survival.3 Good results have also been reported with intravesical BCG,2,4 and meta- analyses5,6 have found it to produce lower recurrence rates than mitomycin. A single dose of intravesical chemother- apy may be given within 24 hours of resection in patients with primary resected low-grade tumours.1 Adjuvant in- travesical therapy with an antineoplastic (usually mitomy- cin) or BCG is recommended for patients with recurrent Ta tumours or primary higher grade T1, and BCG is generally preferred to antineoplastics in primary CIS.1,7 Mainte- nance intravesical BCG therapy for CIS is recommended for those showing a complete response. Those with recur- rent or persistent disease can be given a second course of BCG or mitomycin. If residual disease is still present, cys- tectomy should be considered; intravesical therapy with a different agent (mitomycin, valrubicin, interferon alfa, or BCG plus interferon alfa) is an alternative to cystectomy.
